articles.title: Bhaskar Rao played twenty instruments, and sang in ten languages
articles.deck: He sat in the corner of a room until he was ten. Then a pastor asked whether he wanted to go to school. Our 2012 conversation with the flutist, who died in May.

hero.alt: Bhaskar Rao playing a bamboo flute against a brick wall, wearing dark glasses

interviewMeta.subject: V. Bhaskar Rao
interviewMeta.subjectBio: A flutist and music composer with the Vishwa Vani ministry in Hyderabad, a keyboard tutor, and an electronics engineer who repaired church instruments. He held an MA in flute. He died in May 2026.

archiveMeta.editNote: Published as it appeared in the September 2012 issue, with the column reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected. His own answers are unchanged and stand in the present tense he spoke them in. The magazine's descriptive introduction has been put into the past tense: he died in May 2026. See the note at the head of the piece.

body.v: Bhaskar Rao gave us this interview in September 2012. He died in May 2026, and a funeral bhajan was held for him on 13 May at Lalapet, Secunderabad, where the musicians and singers he had taught and played alongside gathered to sing. We are republishing the conversation as he gave it, in his own words and in the present tense he spoke them in.

Bhaskar Rao was born blind, and was capable of doing any work a sighted person does. He was a musician many times over and a music composer. He held a diploma in electronics and could work with electronic equipment. The 5Talents team got an opportunity to interview him in 2012. In spite of his busy schedule, he spared his time with us, sharing his testimony and his encouragement.

Despite his inability to see, he stepped up to the task. Instead of concentrating on the sight he lacked, he focused on the senses and the health he did have, and raised himself as an educated, well-rounded, talented man who touched a great many people — through his life, and through his music ministry.

Bhaskar had fun wherever he went. He was laid-back and very easy to get along with. Children flocked to him, and he was happy to answer any question they had about his blindness. Most of all, he was a wonderful influence in the lives of a great many people. He inspired both blind and sighted people to realise what they have, instead of looking at what they do not. Things were not always easy for him, but he said that God provided for him whenever he needed it.
“What are the talents you got?”
5Talents: Hello Mr Bhaskar, greetings from 5Talents. How are you?
Praise the Lord! Let all glory be to the Lord. Today whatever I am is because of Him.
5Talents: What are the talents you got?

I did a diploma in music in western, Carnatic and Hindustani, did an M.A. in flute specialization, can play various musical instruments — like keyboard, trumpet, saxophone, clarinet, guitar, tabla, mridangam and mouth organ. I speak and sing in ten languages. I can create more than 300 mimicry voices.
I completed my electronic engineering and can replace micro chip ICs with LED balls of the electronics.
5Talents: Wow, that is amazing. Being a blind person, how is it possible?
People who have vision think that blind people are useless and not capable of doing any work. But to overcome their opinion, I decided to take a step which would prove them wrong.

My father died when I was five. Till the age of ten, I was just sitting in a corner of a room like a doll, and useless. But I was listening to music, which is the only source of knowledge and pleasant to me. I got the strong desire to learn music and the world.

One day a pastor met me and asked me if I wanted to study at school, and I agreed. He enrolled me in the Lutheran School for Blind at Guntur. My life changed from a hopeless blind into a transformed new person. I learned Braille — a system of raised dots which can be read by touch. I did 6 years of diploma in music and further I also did electronic engineering.
Bhaskar Rao has mastered 20 musical instruments. He can speak and sing in ten languages.
“Why should I accept this god?”
5Talents: When did you receive Jesus Christ as your personal saviour?

Surprisingly, even though I studied in a Christian school, I hated Christians. I was brought up in an upper caste family where we worship many gods and goddesses. So I thought that Jesus is a lower caste god, and why should I accept this god?

But one day I realized that I had no relationship with the gods I worshipped in my past life. The priest at the temple didn't even know me, but this pastor cared about me and my life. As I learnt more about Jesus Christ and His sacrifice for my sins and for the entire world's sin, I began to put my faith in Him and started believing Him as only God. I also learnt that Jesus Christ is the resurrection and He has resurrection power, where no other man, gods or goddesses has that power. I accepted Jesus as my personal saviour and Lord and submitted my life to Him.

Today, I proudly say that a blind man like me is capable of doing everything, because I have achieved it in my life through Jesus Christ. It is not me who is doing those things but it is God who works in me. Whatever I do now, it's not me but Jesus Christ in me is doing those mighty things.
“I am specially concerned about youth”
5Talents: How do you use your talents to glorify Jesus?

Currently I am a music composer for a Christian organisation, VishwaVani. I attend musical programmes and gospel meetings to sing and play for the Lord. I am specially concerned about youth; mostly I was invited to speak and encourage among the youth. I am a professional keyboard tutor for western music — students come to me to learn music and vocals. I repair keyboards of any brand; specially church instruments are brought to me.
5Talents: How do you encourage the people who have not discovered their talents, or who would get discouraged by others?

Actually, a person knowing their talent is a specialty. And after discovering the talent, they would use that talent for the Lord's kingdom only after they surrender their life to Christ. Without giving one's life to God a person will never think to use their talent for God, because worldly we would earn a lot of money through the talent.

Dear readers, if you are handicapped, don't despair and don't be discouraged. Take a step toward Jesus and have faith in Him. He will surely transform your life to the great heights as He has done in my life. Today, I am a transformed Bhaskar Rao and God has blessed me with a good wife, children and a status in the society.
It has been 27 years till now. I am using all these talents for His kingdom and for His glory, and will be continuing till the end.
May God bless you. Amen.
Bhaskar Rao kept that promise for a further fourteen years. He died in May 2026, still teaching, still playing.

articles.title: In nine years of ministry I have watched leaders quietly become puppets
articles.deck: The manager who never leaves the chair. The supreme leader who decides by preference. And Elijah, who went from calling down fire to lying under a tree asking to die.

archiveMeta.editNote: Published from the September 2012 issue. Reading order repaired, typographical errors corrected, and the prose lightly tightened by the author's own permission.

body.v: In 9 years of ministry, I see Christian ministry leaders often fall into these categories. A prophet is someone who says what God is saying and does what God is doing. In contrast, there is the puppet.
Puppets have someone or something else pulling the strings of their life.

Sometimes it is the squeaky wheel. In a Christian organisation it is the managers who never want to leave their chairs, complaining constantly about preferences. They choose what kind of staff they want to work with, whom they can control, and how to get work out of them while keeping a limit on their talents.

Some managers hold their position for years. How? When you are talented, innovative, creative, and show the marks of a leader, they suppress your conduct, pull you down and keep you in your place. They take the credit for the good things employees do, and redirect the blame when something goes wrong. That is just a glance at the Christian workplace today.
So, let us see who is the Puppet?
The supreme leader of the organization! And they make decisions on the manager's preferences or their own.
Leaders need to lead out of principle, not preference.
Leaders need to program services by principle, not preference.

If you allow those with the preferences to make the rules, then not only are you a puppet, but according to the Bible, you have become a judge — thus asking God to move off of His throne and let you sit there with your heart that has evil intentions.
Yet, for others, they allow controlling personalities or the spirit of Jezebel to lead their life and ministry.
We have all struggled between the role of prophet and puppet at times.
Elijah

One of the clearest cases in the Bible is that of Elijah. On the mountaintop, he was God's man calling down fire from heaven, proving to his generation that God was indeed God. Then he hears word that Jezebel is after him. He went from prophet to puppet just like that — literally running for his life, and falling under a tree, praying he would die.

Biblical leadership includes direction from above. David says, “He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters… He guides me in the paths of righteousness.” (Ps. 23:2,3) The world assumes people will automatically know the best direction based on following their feelings. God rejects this idea, and instead advances the idea of leadership and authority. In his view, we often need outside direction on which way to go.
Biblical guidance is important in ministry, but we are still left to apply biblical teaching in area after area, and these are often judgment calls requiring wisdom and experience.
Success in ministry can lead to the wrong conclusions
We may conclude that because we succeeded, our ministry methods must have been especially correct.

Meanwhile, our success may be the result of something completely different. Our attribution of success to our superior methods is wrong, but we usually have no way of knowing that until we fail using those same “miracle methods.” The experience of failure throws us into a state of amazement and disillusionment, and this confused state of mind is exactly what God needs to bring us out of our ego-driven paradigm. Only then can we listen to new ideas, new ways of explaining past success, and engage in original thinking for the future to make right decisions.
We must cut ourselves free from those people, as well as preferences, that control and manipulate us in making right decisions.
We must be willing to lead and be the prophet, not a puppet!

articles.title: Every job in a king’s palace has a match in the church
articles.deck: Soldiers, watchmen, messengers, potters, musicians, gardeners, administrators. A theology lecturer runs the whole staff list and asks who you are on it.

archiveMeta.editNote: Published as it appeared in the September 2012 issue. Column reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected; the wording is otherwise the author's.

body.v: Workers of King

The king needs efficient workers to do some special tasks in the palace. The worker should be very sincere, honest and a hard worker. Every worker has their own duties and responsibilities. Below are some of the examples of king's men who are appointed to perform their duties and responsibilities in the royal palace. They are compared with the Kingdom of God, where every one of us has to take the responsibility in His palace.
“…He is Lord of lords and King of kings — and with him will be his called, chosen and faithful followers.” Rev. 17:14
Soldiers — Pastors
“Endure hardship with us like a good soldier of Christ Jesus.” 2 Tim 2:3

They work for the king and fight for the king to extend the kingdom. They guard the king's palace day and night. Similarly, pastors work for the king and fight to establish His kingdom on earth. They also guard His palace 24×7, which is called “Church”.
Watchman — Prayer Warrior
“Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me.” Eze 3:17

Watchmen are of as early a date as cities, robbers and wars. Jerusalem and other cities had regular guards night and day. Prayer warriors are like watchmen. They guard the palace (church) by praying. They pray for individuals, their families, for the sick and for salvation.
Messengers — Evangelists
“…which are now reported unto you by them that have preached the gospel unto you with the Holy Ghost sent down from heaven.” 1 Pet 1:12

Messengers are present to bring and carry news for the king. Messengers also act as communicators between people and the king. Messengers represent evangelists who are mediators between God and the people on this earth. The regular Hebrew word for “messenger” is mal'akh, the Greek aggelos. This may be a human messenger or a messenger of God, an angel.
Potters — Women's Fellowship
“These were the potters and those who dwell at Netaim and Gederah; there they dwelt with the king for his work.” 1 Chron 4:23

Potters prepare vessels for the king for his use. They were probably brick makers, perhaps potters also, who had their dwelling in low grounds, and fabricated the clay into pots and bricks that was digged up in forming fences in the king's palace. Women's fellowship, who are compared with potters, prepare the church kids, youth, elders and believers to be used in the church.
Musicians — Worship Leaders
“…I acquired men and women singers, and a harem as well — the delights of the heart of man.” Eccles 2:8

Musicians play instruments and sing for the king in his royal palace. Their job is to make the king happy and pleased, especially glorifying the king. Similarly, worship leaders are compared to musicians. Worship leaders lead the choir in church during praise and worship. They magnify the Lord for all the miracles He has done. A worship leader connects the congregation to heaven in singing and worshipping.
Gardeners — Sunday School Teachers
“They made me keeper of the vineyards.” Song of Songs 1:6

The gardener plants varieties of plants, herbs and crops in the king's garden. His duty is to check if the plants are well rooted, watered, and to fertilise the ground. The gardener is compared with the Sunday School teacher, and the plants are compared with the students. The Sunday School children should be nurtured with the word of God and in prayer.
Administrators — Church Elders
“…the young men without any physical defect, handsome, showing aptitude for every kind of learning, well informed, quick to understand, and qualified to serve in the king's palace.” Dan 1:4

Administrators govern the other workers to work in the king's palace. They assist the king and direct or manage affairs, execute, or dispense, whether in civil, judicial, political, or ecclesiastical affairs. Church elders are compared to an administrator who manages the church affairs, supporting the pastor in managing the congregation.
Work for King

The workers work for the king to get reward. Also to get the blessings from the king. The workers of the king have the same honour and respect what the king has. Our God is the King of kings, who not only cares for His worker but He loves them, who is now busy preparing a place in His kingdom.

Those who work in the king's palace will never have scarcity. They will be given all the facilities which the king possesses. In 1 Kings 4:22–23 we know thousands of workers of King Solomon were given the best food and they were living a royal life. The king always meets all the physical, spiritual and social needs of a worker.
His palace needs creative and hard workers. The place is not for lazy people.
There is a need of workers in the Kingdom of God. The King has called all of us to be in His palace. There is much to do for His Kingdom. Are you ready to join the crew?
Let us involve in the Church of God. King's palace is nothing but CHURCH. Let's be a worker of the Church and work for the king and live for the king.

articles.title: He fed two thousand children a day and never once asked anyone for money
articles.deck: George Müller was a thief at ten and a fraud at twenty. Then he built five orphanages in Bristol, ran them for sixty years on donations he refused to solicit, and published his accounts so anyone could check him.

archiveMeta.editNote: The 2012 version of this piece was not original work. It has been written again from Müller's own autobiography and from the nineteenth-century biographies, all of which are out of copyright. Sources are listed at the foot.

body.v: This piece was first published in our September 2012 issue. That version has been withdrawn and the story written again from the original sources — Müller's own account of his life, and the biographies written by people who knew him. What follows is new work. The sources are listed at the end.

By the age of ten, George Müller was stealing government money from his father, who was the tax collector. He was good at it. When his father grew suspicious and laid out a marked sum to catch him, Müller found the trap, took part of the money, and hid the rest in his shoe.
At fourteen he was playing cards in a tavern and drinking while his mother lay dying a few streets away. He found out the next morning, walking home.

Sixty years later, five houses on a hill in Bristol were feeding, clothing and schooling around two thousand children at a time. Over his lifetime he cared for 10,024 orphans. He never once asked anybody for a donation.
A boy being trained for a job he did not want

He was born in 1805 in Kroppenstädt, a village in what was then Prussia, and grew up in Heimersleben, where his father collected taxes. His father's ambition for him was specific and entirely financial. The state church paid its clergy well, so George would be a clergyman. He was sent to study divinity at Halle with that in view.

He describes those student years without any softening. He was a thief, a liar and a gambler. He ran up debts, took money from friends on stories he had invented, and was once jailed for skipping out on hotel bills. He had no Bible. He had not read scripture in years. He took communion twice a year out of habit and heard nothing preached that he could remember.
He was, in other words, exactly the kind of person the respectable version of this story would leave out.
The evening in somebody's front room

In 1825 a fellow student named Beta mentioned that a group met in a private house on Saturday evenings to read the Bible, sing, and pray. Müller went, mostly out of curiosity. What struck him was not a sermon. It was watching a man kneel down on the floor to pray.
In his own account of it, written years afterwards, he is careful not to overstate what he understood at the time:
I have no doubt that He began a work of grace in me. Even though I scarcely had any knowledge of who God truly was, that evening was the turning point in my life.
body.highlight: that evening was the turning point

body.v: He went home, knelt by his own bed and asked for help. The drinking, the stealing and the lying stopped. His father, who had paid for an education meant to produce a comfortable salary, was furious when it became clear his son intended to give the salary away.
Refusing to be paid

Müller moved to England in 1829 and settled into pastoral work in Devon, and then in Bristol, where he stayed for the rest of his life. Two decisions from those first years explain everything that followed.

He gave up his salary. He had been on £55 a year at a chapel in Shaldon, and he concluded that a fixed wage collected from the congregation made people give out of obligation rather than because they wanted to. So he stopped taking it and lived on whatever came in unasked.

He also abolished pew rents. Churches at the time sold the good seats, which meant the moneyed families sat at the front by arrangement. Müller read James 2 — the passage about showing deference to the man in fine clothes — decided the practice could not survive it, and ended it.
Neither decision cost him much yet. Both were about to be tested at scale.
Thirty girls, then two thousand children
The orphan work began in 1836 in his own rented house at 6 Wilson Street, Bristol, prepared for thirty girls. Three more houses on the same street followed, and the number in his care reached 130.

By 1845 the neighbours had had enough of the noise and the strain on the street's water supply, and Müller decided to build. The first purpose-built house at Ashley Down opened in 1849 for three hundred children. Four more followed. By 1870 there were 1,722 children living on that hill with room for over two thousand.

The buildings cost more than £100,000, an enormous sum in the 1850s. He never launched an appeal, never wrote to a wealthy man asking for a contribution, and never borrowed. When he needed something he prayed for it and waited, and if it did not come he did not do the thing.

The most famous morning at Ashley Down is famous because it was documented rather than remembered. The children were at the table for breakfast and there was no food in the building. Müller gave thanks for the meal anyway. As they finished, the baker knocked — he had been unable to sleep and had got up at two in the morning to bake for them. Then the milkman's cart broke down directly outside and he handed over his milk rather than let it spoil.
There are hundreds of entries like it in his journals, because he wrote every one of them down as it happened.
The receipts
This is the part that gets left out of the inspirational version, and it is the part that makes the rest credible.
Müller kept accounts obsessively and published them. Every gift was recorded: a single farthing, £3,000, an old teaspoon. He printed his receipts with a standing instruction to the donor:

Donors are requested, kindly to keep the receipts and to compare them with the Supplement to the Report, which records every donation received, so that they may be satisfied that their donations have been properly applied.
body.highlight: so that they may be satisfied

body.v: He was inviting every person who gave him a coin to audit him. The books were open for anyone to inspect and the annual reports listed every transaction. Over his lifetime the institution received and spent £1,381,171, somewhere near £113 million in today's money, and he wanted every line of it checkable.

His own income, all of it unsolicited, reached over £2,000 a year by 1870. He kept about £300 and gave the rest away. He died with an estate of a hundred and sixty pounds, most of it the value of his furniture.
What it cost
Mary, his wife of thirty-nine years and the person who actually ran the orphan houses day to day, died in 1870. He preached at her funeral himself.

He was not universally admired. He was accused of raising poor children above their station. The complaint was that he educated them too well, and that nearby factories and mines could not get workers because he kept finding the children apprenticeships and trades instead. He employed an inspector to keep the teaching standards up. Every child left with a Bible and a tin trunk holding two changes of clothing.

He also spent years inside a bitter split in his own movement. When the Brethren divided in the 1840s, Müller took the position that people should not be excluded for associating with someone whose doctrine was disputed. John Nelson Darby, leading the other side, called on him in July 1849 to talk it over. Müller had appointments and could give him ten minutes. Ten minutes was not enough, and the two men never met again.
Why he is still known

He travelled more than 200,000 miles after he turned seventy, preaching in English, French and German across Europe, America, Australia, India, China and Japan. He returned to Bristol and died there on 10 March 1898, in one of the orphan houses. Ten thousand people came to the funeral, fifteen hundred of them children from the homes he had built.

His biographer William Henry Harding thought the world had got him wrong even then, and that people preferred to remember a kindly old gentleman who was fond of children, which was a way of not having to deal with what he actually claimed. The orphanages were never the point to Müller. They were the evidence.
The work continues. The George Müller Charitable Trust still operates in Bristol and still refuses to fundraise.
So what, in 2026?

Almost everything now runs on asking. Creators ask for subscriptions, charities run campaigns, startups pitch, and every app you open is engineered to request something from you. Asking is not wrong. But it is so completely normal that a man who built a £100,000 institution and refused to send a single appeal letter is genuinely difficult to categorise.

The interesting thing is not that he trusted God for money. Plenty of people say that. It is that he built an audit trail so anyone could check whether it had worked — and then published it for sixty years. He was making a claim that could have been falsified at any point, in public, by a bookkeeper.

That is a rarer kind of confidence than the loud kind, and it is worth more. If you are wondering what to do with what you have, the question Müller kept answering was not how much can I raise. It was: can anyone look at my books?

Sources: Müller's own Autobiography (Centenary Memorial edition, 1905, and the Whitaker House edition of 1984); Arthur Tappan Pierson, George Müller of Bristol (1899); William Henry Harding, The Life of George Müller (1914); Nancy Garton, George Müller and his Orphans (1992); Roger Steer, George Müller: Delighted in God (1997).
